name: Kwaza
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Main word stress in Kwaza is basically on the last syllable of the (extended) root. The extended root may include derivational morphemes, but in principle no inflexional suffixes. [p. 307] ... With respect to criterium d), main word stress tends to occur on the last syllable of the root. If the root is extended with derivational morphemes, main word stress is on the last syllable of the last extension. Main word stress is never on the subject cross-reference morphemes, but it does occur on mood morphemes under specific circumstances, which will be mentioned in Section 1.2. [p. 309]
new_statements.citation: van der Voort, Hein. 2002. The quotative construction in Kwaza and its (de-)grammaticalisation. In M. Crevels, S. van de Kerke, S. Meira & H. van der Voort (eds.), Current Studies on South American Languages (Indigenous Languages of Latin America 3), 307-328. Leiden: Research School of Asian, African, and Amerindian Studies (CNWS).
new_statements.locator: p. 307 (§1 Introduction) and p. 309 (§1.1 Argument agreement)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress goes on the final syllable of the stem, i.e. the root plus any derivational suffixes, and the obligatory inflectional suffixes (subject/object person cross-reference, and usually mood) lie outside the stress domain. So in an uninflected word stress is word-final (the 2004 grammar, per snippet: 'Polysyllabic non-inflected words in isolation always bear main stress on the last syllable'; 'main stress placement is typically on the ultimate syllable'), but in an inflected verb it falls before the inflectional complex, so its position counted from the word edge depends on the morphology. No phonemic tone, length or (per van der Voort 2000) phonemic stress; apparent minimal pairs for stress are morphologically explained (2004 snippet).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described in the 2002 article beyond notation (fn. 2, p. 308: ["] marks a syllable with secondary stress). The 2004 grammar (Google Books snippet, page-less, running head p. 70) says 'every other syllable usually gets automatic rhythmic stress, which is normally not as heavy as the main stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Mood morphemes may carry main stress under specific conditions; negative -he-, future -nã- and the imperative 'usually attract word stress' (2002, p. 310); in quotative (double-inflection) constructions main stress is on the last syllable of the primary layer of inflexions (2002, p. 314); the 2004 grammar (snippets) adds that in running discourse stress varies with pragmatic factors, that word stress can produce stress clash with adjacent words, and that 'wrong' stress patterns are rejected by speakers.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: the domain is the phonological word minus the inflectional suffixes (the '(extended) root'); statement based on field data 1995-1998 and elicited/isolation forms; running-discourse variation is pragmatic (2004 snippet).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single Kwaza (Koaiá) language of the Tubarão-Latundê reserve, Rondônia (kwaz1243); no dialect issue. Speakers reportedly contrast their ultimate-syllable stress with penultimate stress in neighbouring Aikanã (aika1237) per a 2004 snippet.

sources.note: p. 41: 'Kwaza has no phonemic tone, stress or length. Because the exact rules for stress placement have not yet been established I have indicated main word stress by an apostrophe [\'] that precedes the stressed syllable in a polysyllabic word.' No rule given.
